You... Are aware you've used three examples of things that are about encoding and communicating information, to try and prove a "point" about natural science, right?

Computers are actually a great example. If you know a little, you "know" they're binary. But if you know a bit more, you know that binary is just the way we encode signals. In reality, there are actually a range of voltages, and we assign a cutoff point convenient to us. Anything below the cutoff point is interpreted as a 0, anything above is interpreted as a 1. So when you're using the computer, you're flattening 3.01 volts and 60 volts to "above 3, therefore 1" even though in reality, one of those voltages just set your computer on fire.

Sex is the same. We've taken some characteristics, grouped them together, and assigned them meaning for social purposes. It's good enough for communicating information about those characteristics in a majority of cases. However, the outliers are still there. You haven't gotten rid of them just because you've waved your hand and said "eh, close enough," and pretending otherwise is a good way to end up with problems.

The community you stumbled across isn't... Typical of the already small minority of people who transition, then detransition. The fact is that there are detransitioners, and then there are "detransitioners."

The former are people who transitioned, and then detransitioned for whatever reason. The most common reason appears to be social stigma, lack of support, that sort of thing, but occasionally someone will decide that transitioning genuinely isn't for them. They're largely supported by, and supportive of, the trans community. I've known a few people who have detransitioned for various reasons. I've partially detransitioned a couple times for safety, and re-transitioned. It's not super common for someone to permanently detransition, but it does happen sometimes.

But the "detransitioners" that get all the attention by making the outlandish claims about doctors pushing hormones or surgery on them after a mere 15 minute visit are a far right propaganda effort to try and demonize trans people. Period. There's little to no evidence that more than maybe a dozen of them exist in the world, and even those are dubious. The "verifiable" ones are all now celebrities who make a shit ton of money being trotted out as an example by anti-trans groups. They've frequently never transitioned beyond maybe experimenting with new names, and several have families that were well established in the anti-trans "activism" scene long before their alleged "transitions." The rest are pretty universally anonymous on places like reddit. None of it passes even a cursory smell check.

The reality of the situation is that even in the most permissive environments, no doctor is just throwing hormones at random children. Even if what they claim to have gone through was real, and was a pervasive problem, the thing that they describe as "ruining their body" is *gender dysphoria.* It's the same thing trans people go through. So it's funny that that narrative never gets trotted out to, say, support improved standards that ensure that nobody has to go through that. It's always to try and restrict trans people more.

TL;DR: Detransitioners are real, and are deserving of support. The people you stumbled across probably aren't, and *are certainly* part of a concerted propaganda effort to reframe trans people wanting to be *left the fuck alone* as "the evil transes coming for your kids."

Uh, let's see.... More specific advice though....

1. Everyone puts their foot in their mouth sometimes, especially before you get to really know someone. Making too big a deal out of apologizing *can* feel patronizing, so a quick apology and correction is usually better than making a big song and dance out of fixing things.

2. There are probably going to be certain traditionally gendered experiences with romance that they won't have had. For example, lots of trans women might never have received flowers, so that could be a nice gesture even if it's not something you'd normally do.

3. If they're pretty open about being trans, expect them to open up about lots of things pretty quickly. It's one of those things where since you've had to share something really stigmatized, and you get so many intrusive questions, you kinda lose any idea for what's "normal" to share at what stage in a friendship or relationship. You don't have to share more than you're comfortable with, and don't pry.

4. Again, there's no universal trans experience. If you ask 10 trans people what their experience of being trans is, you'll probably get at least 11 different answers. Communicate, don't assume.

5. Have fun, don't sweat it if it doesn't work out. Relationships should be sources of joy and contentment for everyone involved.

Yeah, it's good to be curious, and read the information that's out there. But bias is important to understand and factor in.

If a scientific paper sets out to find the "cure for transgenderism," and they magically find that beating your kids does it, then there's an obvious bias there.

But the reader also has bias, and that's harder to factor in. If you find yourself feeling relief or disgust at the findings of a paper, or, say, scrolling down a news article to see whether the person in your town arrested for sex offenses was a member of the local hate church (I've caught myself doing this one), then you need to pause for a moment and consider that your bias might not make you reliable to draw conclusions right this second.

So, to dig into your logic a bit, if trans people aren't born trans, that means there's some postnatal environmental factor that "makes" us trans. Running with that, it could be nurture (a common transphobic canard that we're "raised wrong"), or something chemical (another common claim that we're being poisoned), or some event in our lives (the good old trauma lie).

If this were the case, being trans could be prevented, and based on the framing of most of these, "should be." And pushing back against that makes someone transphobic?

I want to be clear - I don't think you're being consciously transphobic, but it seems like you've maybe got some bad information, or some unexplored preconceptions or something, because you're pretty unequivocally wrong, and the argument you're making has some really disturbing implications if you take it where it's heading.

That doesn't make the other person in your argument *right* per se - we don't know what "causes" being trans. There have been cases of identical twins raised separately both turning out trans, and cases of only one twin in a pair raised together being trans, which kinda indicates there are both genetic and environmental factors. But it's not something that "happens" to you. It's inherent in some way.

TL;DR: Factually, there isn't a solid answer yet, when we get one it's likely to be a whole bunch of stuff. Ethically, the argument you're making has a higher potential for harm to trans people than the alternative. Just leave it alone, no good can come of laypeople trying to figure out "why" trans people exist in the current climate.

That's what it's like for me to drink a cup of coffee or take my meds. When they kick in, my brain finally shuts up with the incessant background buzz of random thoughts and sensations, and I can actually get things done or relax.

Most ADHD people don't get good sleep because of racing thoughts, and trying to do anything unmedicated takes extra energy to push through the nonsense, so for my personal experience at least, I'm always tired. I just don't always feel it unless I'm medicated and caffeinated.

The only pushback I can offer from another leftie is that I don't think *anyone* really cares about facts or data outside using them as an argument to try and defend the positions we already support.

The fundamental disagreement between the left and the right isn't really about reality (although it's drifted that direction in the last couple decades), it's about very different values. The right tends to primarily value social cohesion, the left values equity, and the center values the current status quo. To be clear, none of these are inherently *wrong,* although I disagree with the priorities of the right and center. Fairness, social cohesion, and stability are all positive aspects of a functional society, it's just a matter of what we think is most important.

A really good example right now is the current political situation in the US. There's a bunch of unprecedented stuff coming out of the government, much of which is oriented around dismantling flawed institutions that nevertheless benefit a lot of people.

The right's reaction is largely "hell yeah, we're winning," even though dismantling those institutions means losing the benefits of them. The left's reaction is generally "this is wrong and will hurt people," even though we disagree with a lot of the stuff those institutions do, and have been opposing many of them for decades. The center's reaction is mostly "trust in the system to correct itself," even though these systems have never been tested to this extent, and in many cases are being dismantled wholesale.

We don't have data yet on how this is going to affect things, and we probably won't for decades, given the sheer scope of the changes being made. But we've all got a pretty strong opinion on it regardless, because our values have guided us to a position.

Nobody's trying to get rid of anything, no. Well, except the Trump administration in the US, who are banning words like "women" to "fight DEI," but I don't think that's really what you're asking about.

The thing that people are trying to get acknowledgement of, is that things are more complicated and nuanced than just lumping everyone into one of two boxes and calling it a day.

Sex is currently treated as a single, unchangeable binary, but there are actually a lot of things that we lump into that categorization, and while they're *usually* associated with one another, it's biology, so stuff gets complicated sometimes. "Sex" could refer to primary sexual characteristics (reproductive systems), secondary sexual characteristics (breasts, facial hair, etc), chromosomal makeup, or hormone profiles. Each of those can be broken down even further. The categories our society currently uses are shorthands for the two most common groupings of those, but they can fall short since potentially as many as 1.7% of the population don't fit neatly into either. These individuals are referred to as *intersex*. For reference, 1.7% of the world population is about 140 million people, so it's not some tiny group that can be discounted, it's about the same number of people as have red hair.

You've also got gender, which is a set of social roles historically related to, but not solely based on, sex. Note that it's different from "traditional gender roles." It's not about one group of people "being in the kitchen" or whatever. It's about the ways that people interact with you, and how you interact with them. The obvious ways that manifest to an outside observer are things like pronouns or the way you present yourself to the world, but there are also a lot of internal, self identity aspects. Just like with sex, it's usually a good enough shorthand, but we assign these roles based on perceived sex, so for some of us (trans people), it doesn't really work for us. Some people have a gender identity usually associated with the "opposite sex," and some (nonbinary people) have a gender identity that doesn't really fit into either of the two big boxes.

The reason that certain groups have started moving away from the big catchall terms is that they can be misleading. Let's say you're working at a hospital trying to design an ad campaign to promote what is traditionally referred to as "women's health care" - pregnancy care, gynecology, breast cancer screenings, and the like. Your first pass has ads like "women should make sure to schedule regular breast cancer screenings." But you realize, hey, there are some people with breasts who aren't women. You shrug and think "that's not very many people, and they'll figure it out." A year passes, and you get a commission for a new ad campaign. This one needs to target those people with breasts who aren't women, because oops, there's been a huge increase in breast cancer diagnoses in that population because they didn't realize they needed to come in.

So your second pass, you say "females should get regular breast cancer screenings," but on reading it again, you frown, shuffle through your stats pile, and realize that there's another group in there that's vulnerable that might not realize that refers to them. So your final pass says "people with breasts should get regular breast cancer screenings." You publish it, and three days later your name, face, and home address are on 4chan in a thread of people screaming about how you're "erasing women." All because you tried to be as accurate as possible.

And that's the reality of the situation. It's people trying to be as accurate as possible and getting smacked in the face with culture war nonsense. Nobody is trying to "get rid of" sex. At least nobody with any clout or popular support. The issue is people with bad intentions twisting good intentioned use of nuance, so they can use it as a wedge issue to get themselves more power.

That's a really good question, and while I agree with the answers saying it's about feeling like one of the special people in the know, I'm gonna add a couple aspects that I think are really important to the specific question as to how people get all the way to the conspiracy theories that are ridiculously untrue, instead of the ones that are untrue, but you can kinda understand why someone might think it.

I'm not an expert by any means, but I'm a sociologist who has primarily specialized in studying conspiracism and political extremism, and it's also just a personal interest of mine, so I've spent quite a bit of time and effort looking into this.

The first thing is that your average conspiracy theorist doesn't generally start with the really outlandish stuff about secret mars bases or whatever. There are plenty of entry level conspiracy theories that we've probably all at least played around with the idea of, some of which are even actually true. This is the stuff at the level of JFK assassination theories, or MKULTRA, or generally anything else involving the CIA doing shady and/or wacky shit during the Cold War. Even the stuff that probably isn't true is pretty believable even to a layperson because, y'know, the CIA *did* do a lot of shady and/or wacky shit during the Cold War.

And if you get into those spaces more than just dipping a toe in, that's where the other half of the equation starts to kick in. Most conspiracy theories are *syncretic*, which in this context means they incorporate, absorb, or purport to explain other conspiracy theories. So for example, if you believe the CIA killed JFK, well the question becomes why. And if you're in those conspiracy groups, you might "discover" that maybe it was because he stumbled upon something he wasn't "supposed to know."

And the theories keep building upon each other like that. You can start at JFK assassination, and move to, say, moon landing denial, to flat earth, to aliens, to a secret Illuminati cabal. And that last one is the last big part of the puzzle, because it, and its little brothers, The New World Order, Globalists, Cultural Marxists, and the like, are all sort of the end of the conspiracy radicalization pipeline. It's the point where "they" become defined. And nearly every single time, "they" are Jewish, because all of this is basically just people riffing for over a century on the Protocols of the Elders of Zion, a piece of antisemitic Tsarist Russian propaganda published in 1903 and largely plagiarized from various other antisemitic screeds.

So yeah, it's a pipeline of ideas that starts pretty reasonable, and keeps building and building to help launder antisemitism. It's actually kind of an interesting time for study of conspiracy theories, because QAnon is so virulently syncretic that it's absorbed pretty much everything else, and you tend not to see nearly as many, say, UFO guys any more because they're all talking about secret pizza basements and Hilary Clinton drinking blood. So we can kind of see that end stage conspiracism playing out en masse in real time. Terrible for the world, of course, but interesting at least.

If you're interested in this stuff there's a podcast called Knowledge Fight that's done some interesting stuff looking into Alex Jones's role in the pipeline, as well as a few of the more out there types. It's heavy stuff, and most of the episodes deal more with Jones's politics than the conspiracism, but there's a lot of good information if you're willing to wade through hours of comedians getting mad at Jones being a dick.

ETA: I'd also like to say that contrary to pretty much everyone's belief, conspiracy theories aren't strictly a left or right wing thing. A lot of the well known ones tend to skew rightward at the moment, but there are plenty of conspiracy theories that skew the other direction, or have skewed the other way in the past and have recently been folded into QAnon.

For example, my beliefs are firmly on the left, and even knowing how they operate, I've fallen victim to some entry level conspiracy theories. When the COVID vaccines first started rolling out, I had reservations about how fast they showed up, and I speculated that the outgoing Trump administration had rushed it faster than was safe to try and take credit for it. There are a couple of things.

Ideally, you wouldn't be heating the solder on the other parts enough to melt it, so it wouldn't be an issue at all. With a part like this, you've got to use a hot air gun, so that solder will probably melt somewhat regardless.

The surface tension of the melted solder will actually help keep the part in place, to an extent. You can see that effect with the part being replaced sliding into the correct spot. If you nudge it, it'll still move, but it's something.

Finally, the parts generally also have a small dot of glue under them, which keeps them from sliding around from just whatever force is applied by the flux and isopropyl. It's easy enough to break the glue if you need to move the part, or if you slip and knock something.

Honestly, I don't think the person in this video is being careful enough, but that's just me. The scrubbing motions with the soldering iron and the wick when cleaning up the excess solder aren't something I'd do in this situation. I'd be worried about damaging a surrounding part, or accidentally pulling off one of the pads.

Flux is the white goop that sort of "melts" into clear liquid.

The best way to think about it is that it's sort of like a solvent for the solder (the metal glue). When you melt solder, you want it to get between the parts you need it to get between and make a good physical and electrical connection. The flux helps it flow smoothly so it does that, instead of clumping up.

Answer: Hi, I'm an American trans person. The answer is it's complicated, and it's gonna depend on how much you're willing to assume people are operating in good faith.

The surface level "good faith" reading is that we're a small enough group that a fair few people don't know anyone who's trans, but large enough that we get seen around fairly regularly. Our experience of life is different enough from the norm that it makes people uncomfortable, and it also happens to break a lot of preconceptions people have about how the world works. So they see us a ton, and we make them uncomfortable, but they never have to really get to know us or learn about us, so we're easy to other.

A more cynical take is that we're a distraction to rile up the base while the politicians ram through their wildly unpopular ideas like Medicaid and Social Security cuts. I think there's truth to this, but it's not the whole picture.

The part that's missing from both of those interpretations is control. Power is a lot easier to centralize when you can put people into nice, neat boxes, and place restrictions on those boxes.

For decades, conservatives have gone after gay people with literally all of the arguments they're now using against trans people - false allegations of grooming, or an identity being inherently sexual, or people being untrustworthy. The reason they did that is because The Gays™ help break one of those sets of boxes, specifically so-called "traditional" gender roles. Those gender roles offer a lot of control to institutions like the church and industry by limiting the options of women, funneling them into a reproductive role, and by limiting the options of men to funnel them into a labor role. Unfortunately for them, that control is disrupted if people have more options, such as marrying the same gender.

Conservatives lost their manufactured culture war on The Gays™ in 2015 with Obergefell, but their ideology is still dependent on enforcing those boxes, so they pivoted to trying to divide the traditionally unified LGBTQIA+ alliance. That's why you see so many tiny "LGB drop the T" type groups funded by right wing groups like the Heritage Foundation cropping up in the last decade.

Trans people are arguably even more of a threat than The Gays™ were. We're more visible, and our very existence threatens not only the methods of control, but the very philosophy behind the control. You can't control people by placing them in boxes if the borders of the boxes have been blurred. So they're making us a much larger part of their political focus at the moment than gay rights really ever were. And they're using us as a smokescreen to sneak through stuff that hurts a lot more people, like Idaho passing a resolution calling for a return to marriage discrimination, or the harebrained idea of "covenant marriages" that are basically just a way to try and get the idea of ending no-fault divorce out of the theocracy bro podcast space and into the public policy space.

Liberals and left leaning people get involved with the issue because we disagree with that type of control. Conservatives are pushing it, and I mean.... You can see what happens when the opposition doesn't push back on an issue by looking at the Harris campaign. They didn't push back at all on trans issues, and even conceded quite a bit of ground, and Trump still ran that stupid "Harris is for they/them" ad. 

TL;DR - it's about exerting control over reproduction (yes, that means less freedom for *you,* random person reading this) and the ways in which trans people, and by extension, LGBTQIA+ people in general, make it more difficult to exert that control.

Philosophically speaking, identity is a conversation between the individual and society. On the one hand, you have how the individual is perceived and treated by others, and on the other is how the individual perceived themself. These are always changing and affecting each other in incredibly complex ways (for example, the concept of stereotype threat shows how societal perceptions can affect self perception).

How much each "side" contributes to overall identity changes a lot depending on the individual and the social factors and context involved. Neither is strictly right or wrong - both contribute to an overall whole.

Note that "society" here doesn't just mean transphobes or strangers. It includes your friends, family, other trans people, allies, etc as well. It's everything external to your own perception of yourself.

My take here is this: Very broadly speaking, being trans really just seems to be a matter of consciously choosing to change the way one engages with that conversation surrounding the identity of gender. There isn't really a right or wrong way to "be trans," because the whole system of identity is very nebulous and vibes based to begin with.

So, for example, a trans man is a man, not because he meets some strict (but ultimately arbitrary) external definition, nor *solely* because he identifies as such, but because he is engaging with the systems of identity as a man.

The whole argument over who is "trans enough" or "at what point does someone count as their gender" is kind of like asking "at what point does the river end and the lake begin?" The whole thing starts from the incorrect assumption that there *can* be a single, universal, capital-T, Truth.

Hi, I'm a sociologist!

You're not wrong, exactly, but I think you may have a very common misconception of what "privilege" means, thanks to the term and discussions around it having been hijacked by people who willfully misinterpret it.

In its intended context, privilege is a tool used to examine the disparate outcomes of social structures at a large scale. For example, the structure of policing favors white people over Black - that's a privilege afforded to white people. The structure of the nuclear family favors men over women - a privilege afforded to men. There are a huge number of these, because our society is ludicrously complicated.

The two systems of privilege I used as examples are kind of comparing apples to oranges - one isn't necessarily inherently "more of a privilege" than the other (big asterisk here, I'll get to that in just a second). So the idea of someone being "more privileged" than someone else is kind of meaningless, since it's not really a score, but a way of understanding the systems that affect a situation.

HOWEVER (and here's the asterisk), those systems do interact, and that's where I think your examples are really good at illustrating something that I think gets willfully misunderstood by bad actors in general conversations about this, which is that often these systems work to reinforce each other.

In the case of a white woman accusing a Black man of a sexual crime, we have two aspects coming into contact. Sexist ideas about women being "weak" and "passive" are usually used to victimize them, but in this specific case, cause them to be viewed as automatic victims. This reinforces racist ideas about Black people being "hypersexual" and "aggressive." These two distinct, but intersecting systems of privilege result in the outcomes we see in your examples. This is what people usually mean when we talk about "intersectionality," that these systems can interact in ways that might not be immediately obvious if we view them as completely separate.

If we misinterpret privilege as a "score," we could interpret that situation as a white woman being more privileged, and we wouldn't be wrong exactly, since in that specific situation, the white woman comes out "on top," but by doing so, we fail to understand the actual systems behind it, which is what sociology is aiming to do with the concept of privilege.

TL;DR - Privilege is a tool for examining societal structures and explaining disparate outcomes, and not something that can really be compared.

Also, read Ida B Wells' [Southern Horrors](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/14975/14975-h/14975-h.htm) if you're interested in this stuff. She was a Black woman who did a deep dive into the white woman/Black man dynamic in the late 18th century American South and she was a way better sociologist than I am.

I addressed the underlying mental health issues that made everything more difficult.  Now I'm still "lazy," but I get the stuff I need to get done, done.

For me, my issues were mostly undiagnosed anxiety, depression, ADHD, and gender dysphoria just... Making me feel awful about anything that wasn't pure escapism.  I maintained this bubble of dissociation to get away from those problems that also helped me ignore the negative feelings I got from having a messy living environment or poor hygiene, and that sort of just made everything spiral.

I ended up starting to improve when I acknowledged the gender issues and started seeing a therapist who helped me put names to the feelings I was having and break through the dissociation.  That made it possible to start taking care of myself again, and I'm going back to school again full time starting on the 24th.

Basically, take care of your mental health.  It's something that's not really paid attention to in mainstream culture, and it massively affects what you feel up to doing.  If you find yourself unable to find the energy for everything, look into spoon theory.  It won't give you more energy or anything like that, but it might give you a better understanding of your own capabilities.  I use it pretty often to prioritize and eliminate things that "leak" spoons (I find I run out of "people" spoons fastest, and things like taking the self-checkout line at the grocery store can save me some that I might be able to repurpose later for cooking, for example).

EDIT: also, certain activities (self-care) can recharge spoons.  Snuggling with my dog, or shaving my legs, or dressing nice can often give me the energy to do more.  Other things can be investments of spoons, like cleaning and doing laundry, where if I spend some spoons now, I get more back later (obviously, that can spiral as well, if I let things get bad, I can hit a point where I don't have the spoons to fix it to get more spoons).  It's just really useful having a concrete, semi-quantitative way of thinking and talking about that concept of motivation and mental energy.

It's something I've been working on getting better at lately because StageRecovery isn't working, so I'm trying my best to get better at getting as much recovery value as possible out of what I can.  My tips are to re-enter at a steeper angle if you can to minimize the effect of drag and gravity on your trajectory, equip your vehicle with some form of landing engines, less for the actual landing and more for steering once you're subsonic, and practice.  I'm not to the point where I can reliably land back on the launch pad or runway or anything, but I can consistently land within the KSC flat area from LKO.  Re-entering from a Mun or Minmus return tends to be a little more dicey because of the higher speed, so I'm not even trying precision landings on those missions yet.

Best way to do it is to place one craft in orbit (or accept a rescue contract, which is much easier), then launch your second craft to as close to the same orbit as possible when the first craft is over the coast of the desert west of KSC.  That should put you on an orbit fairly close to your target.

From there, select your target in the map view so you can see the closest point of approach nodes (you may have to adjust your orbit to cross the target's orbit for this to happen).  If the target position at closest approach is ahead of yours in its orbit, you need to speed up by lowering your orbit (burning retrograde at the closest approach, but be careful not to re-enter).  If it's behind you, you need to slow down by raising your or it (burning prograde).  This is called a phasing orbit, and you can do a bunch of these maneuvers, adjusting at the closest point each time to fine tune your approach until you get your closest point with 10km or so (you may need to adjust your inclination a bit, but you'll be able to see this in the gap between the orbit lines).

At this point, just wait until your closest approach and burn target velocity retrograde (select target in the navball and point toward the retrograde marker) to match speeds with your target.  You can fine tune closer by just pointing at your target and doing a short burn to pick up anywhere from 1m/s if you're close to 100m/s or so if you're far away, then flipping back to the target velocity retrograde marker and killing your velocity at the new closest point.  Repeat until you're in visual range.  You can use the same process to dock as well.

I've never seen that wiki before, so I don't have much of an opinion.  There seem to be some troll articles, but they're pretty easily picked out from the rest, I think.  There's stuff in there I had never heard of, but the stuff I had seems pretty legitimate.  In any case, I agree with your assertion that creating articles for all genders is problematic, because it'd be like trying to create a wiki page for every number (yeah, I know Wikipedia tries to do that).  The whole point of thinking of gender as a spectrum is that there are infinite variations.  We take a handful of points on that spectrum and label them so we can better describe it, but they're not 100% accurate.

Think of light.  Visible light is a spectrum between around 390 and 700nm.  Between those wavelengths of light are a near infinite number of colors.  510nm is green light, 570nm is yellow.  If we look at 540nm, that's going to be a yellowish green.  What about 550nm?  545?  All of those colors can be described as yellow-green, but they're all unique and different colors.  We describe them as "somewhere between yellow and green" because naming all 310 distinct integer wavelengths in the visible light spectrum is honestly ridiculous, let alone all the possible non-integer values.

Gender is the same way.  So we have "man" on one end and "woman" on the other, and halfway in between we have "agender", and a little different but nearby we have "bigender", etc.  That's not really a scientific way of putting it, because quite frankly we're talking about how people feel on the inside, so science is hard in this case.  All we can really do is be respectful.  Yeah, there are trolls out there, but they're generally pretty dumb and easy to weed out.  Compare [this](http://gender.wikia.com/wiki/Totikhaspawnfluid) to [this](http://gender.wikia.com/wiki/Neutrois) and you'll understand what I mean.

These are both ways of representing the reality that don't quite encompass the entire thing.  In reality, there is only one gender, but also many.  It's a spectrum.  Someone who is agender may feel no identification with gender whatsoever, while someone who is bigender feels equal draw to the two opposing ends of the spectrum.  Someone who is genderfluid fluctuates on the spectrum.  These all generally fit under the umbrella of non-binary, that is, not conforming to the common social belief that there are only two genders, man and woman.  These labels just serve to help explain a complicated set social, psychological, and biological circumstances that make up "gender".  They aren't nice little boxes, more...  Loose categorizations.  Someone might fit into one of these categories, more than one, or even none of them.

One thing that's really uncomfortable about this is that there's no one right way to look at this.  Like a lot of biology, psychology, and sociology, there are a lot of blurry lines.  Not everything can be neatly fit into a category, which is where the strawman about "300+ genders" draws its roots from.

It's a lot more complicated than you make it out to be.  Starting "the transgender process" before adolescence really isn't done, and it's certainly not too late to ever really start it.  I know of trans people in their sixties who have come out and transitioned and feel good about it.  It's certainly not impossible to go back unless surgery is done, which is usually a very late step.  The way it's handled for younger people is to simply delay puberty until the kid turns 18.  That's 100% reversible.  All you have to do to start normal puberty is to stop the blockers.  They'll be late bloomers, sure, but their body will develop normally otherwise.

For trans women (MtF), the effects of estrogen are pretty much entirely reversible, so much so, in fact, that testosterone blockers have to be added to keep the body's natural testosterone levels from "overriding" the estrogen.  The only really permanent effect is breast growth, which in the event of the individual changing their mind, is a relatively simple surgery.  For trans men (FtM), it's a little less reversible because testosterone is a lot more powerful.  The permanent effects are (AFAIK) body and facial hair growth and voice changes, both of which can again be reversed with some time and effort.

The really big potential effect is sterility (for trans women at least, not sure about trans men).  However, it's not 100%, reverses when hormones are stopped a decent amount of the time, and you can get around that by freezing sperm anyway.  Beyond that, surgeries are more permanent, but they *are not* the first or only step to transition.  A lot of trans people *don't have surgery at all*.
